newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-SAMPRAS MISSES OUT ON HUGE CHRISTMAS BONUS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS MISSES OUT ON HUGE CHRISTMAS BONUS.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras has decided against flying to Munich to pick up one of the most lucrative Christmas bonuses in sport at this week's Grand Slam Cup.

But his late withdrawal, together with fellow-Americans Todd Martin and Michael Chang, will give Britain's Tim Henman, Swede Thomas Enqvist and Swiss Jakob Hlasek a chance to cash in on their good form during the year.

Sampras could have earned $250,000 just for turning up at the $6 million tournament which brings together the best performers of the year from the four grand slams -- Wimbledon and the Australian, French and U.S. Opens.

As U.S. Open champion, Sampras was guaranteed the bonus together with Australian Open champion Boris Becker, French Open winner Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek who are all playing.

Even if the American, who won a dramatic five-set final against Becker in last month's ATP world championship, had lost in the first round he would have walked away from the southern German city with the first-round loser's cheque of $100,000.

But officials said on Sunday both Sampras and Chang were pulling out of the event because of ankle problems while Martin had a long-standing elbow injury. Henman, Enqvist and Hlasek, who could have earned $50,000 as replacements, can now double their money at least.
When the 16-man knockout tournament was first set up in 1990, some players refused to compete, saying the money on offer was "obscene".
The event, which has been criticised in the past as being just a lucrative exhibition, has since become an established part of the tennis year and most of the top players turn up.
Next season it will be played two months earlier in the year, shortly after the U.S. Open, the last grand slam. Organisers hope that it will then have more credibility as a grand slam showdown.
But this is far from certain. Despite the change of date, Sampras said last month that he would only play in 1997 if he won one of the grand slams.
When asked why, he immediately talked about the $250,000 bonus. The American has earned an astonishing $5.3 million in prize money in Munich since 1990.
Money is effectively one of the tournament's main problems in getting to a level where it can be talked about in the same breath as Wimbledon and the three Opens.
When it started, organisers needed to pay out the biggest money in tennis to make sure the top players turned up at the end of the year when they are usually taking a break from the intense circuit.
In some players' minds, the cash is clearly still the most important factor. Prize money, by contrast, is pretty irrelevant at Wimbledon or Roland Garros where the prestige of winning is paramount.
If the event wants to be regarded as a real grand slam showdown, some believe it should be played on different surfaces every year, such as the grand slams.

Henman will open his campaign against former Wimbledon champion Michael Stich on Tuesday while Becker, a clear favourite on the fast indoor circuit after Sampras's withdrawal, takes on Australian Jason Stoltenberg in the first round.
